title: Sleep helps learning
keyIdea: Your brain keeps working while you sleep: it stores what you practised in the day, so it is still there tomorrow. When it is late, a good night's sleep helps more than one more page of the same thing. Children aged 6 to 12 need 9 to 12 hours a night, so count back from waking up, finish practice in time for bed, and stop screens an hour before lights out.
familyTip: At bedtime, ask: “What did you practise today?” Then say, “Your brain will work on that while you sleep.” In the morning, ask for a quick check of one thing. If homework runs late, choose sleep over one more page of the same work. Together, count back from wake-up time to find a bedtime that gives at least 9 hours.

visual.caption: Does it help learning stick, or get in the way? Drag each card, or tap it and then tap a box.

items: Stay up late doing the same page again
Go to bed at the same time most nights
Play a tablet game in bed
A quick check in the morning
Skip sleep to practise more before a test

lab.caption: Flagship lab: watch the night shift store your practice, run Ava’s and Ben’s nights, count back to a bedtime, sort habits, then plan tonight.

kid: Today you practised your spellings and your 7 times table. Then you went to sleep. Your body rested, but your brain kept working. It went over what you practised and stored it, so it is still there in the morning.
Ava practised, then went to bed. Ben did the same page again and stayed up late. Ava will likely remember more. Ben had less sleep, so his brain had less time to store, and he woke up tired.
Most children your age need 9 to 12 hours of sleep a night. To find your bedtime, start at the time you wake up and count back. If you wake at 7:00 am, 10 hours back is 9:00 pm.

Sleep does not replace practice. You need both: practise first, then sleep. Finish your practice before bedtime, and turn off screens an hour before lights out. In the morning, check one thing you practised.
adult: Ages 8 to 9. Sleep after learning helps memories last: during sleep, and especially deep slow-wave sleep, the brain replays and strengthens what was learned that day (Diekelmann and Born 2010; Rasch and Born 2013). Children gain at least as much from this as adults do (Wilhelm et al. 2013). In a classic study, 9 to 12 year olds who slept about an hour less a night for three nights did worse on attention and memory tasks (Sadeh, Gruber and Raviv 2003).

The American Academy of Sleep Medicine consensus (Paruthi et al. 2016) recommends 9 to 12 hours a night for ages 6 to 12, and the NHS advises a regular bedtime routine and no screens in the hour before bed. The lab turns this into steps a child can do: see that the brain works at night, compare a night of sleep with a late night of the same practice, count back from waking to a bedtime, sort habits, and plan an evening.

Common mistakes: thinking the brain switches off at night; believing that more late practice always beats sleep; treating sleep as lost study time; thinking sleep can replace practice; getting bedtime sums wrong by counting forward instead of back; and finishing with a game or screen right at lights out. Be careful with the lab's memory shelf: it is a picture of the idea, not a measurement. Real memory does not move in neat steps each hour.
This lesson is about why sleep helps learning. The lesson Eating, sleeping and moving to grow covers sleep for growing bodies, and Sleep, screens and wellbeing covers teenage sleep and body clocks.

practice.prompt: What does your brain do while you sleep?
practice.hint: Think about the memory shelf in the lab.
practice.explain: Your brain stores what you practised, so it is still there in the morning.

practice.prompt: You go to bed {n} hours before midnight and wake up at 7:00 am. How many hours of sleep do you get?
practice.hint: Count the hours to midnight ({n}), then add the 7 hours from midnight to 7:00 am.
practice.explain: {n} hours to midnight and 7 more to 7:00 am make {=n+7} hours.

practice.prompt: It is bedtime. Lia has practised her spellings. What helps her remember them best?
choices: Do the same page again for an hour
practice.hint: When does the brain store what you practised?
practice.explain: Go to sleep now. Sleep gives her brain time to store the spellings.

practice.prompt: Ava slept {n} hours. Ben stayed up late and slept {k} hours less. How many hours did Ben sleep?
practice.hint: Start with Ava’s {n} hours and take away {k}.
practice.explain: {n} take away {k} is {=n-k} hours. Less sleep means less time for the brain to store what he practised.

practice.prompt: Does sleep mean you do not need to practise?
choices: No, you need practice and sleep
practice.hint: Sleep stores what you practised. What if you practised nothing?
practice.explain: You need both. Sleep stores practice. It does not replace it.

pool.prompt: Tom says, “Sleep is wasted time. I could be learning.” Is he right?
choices: No, sleep helps you keep what you learned
Yes, so sleep as little as you can
pool.hint: What does the brain do at night?
pool.explain: No. Sleep is when your brain keeps what you learned in the day.

pool.prompt: How many hours of sleep do most children aged 6 to 12 need?
pool.hint: Think of a whole day of 24 hours. Children need close to half of it.
pool.explain: 9 to 12 hours a night, say sleep experts.

pool.prompt: You wake at 7:00 am and need 10 hours of sleep. When should you go to bed?
pool.hint: Start at 7:00 am and count back 10 hours.
pool.explain: Counting back 10 hours from 7:00 am lands on 9:00 pm.

pool.prompt: There is a test tomorrow. What is the best plan?
choices: Practise today, then get a good sleep
Stay up very late to practise
pool.hint: You need two things. Which plan has both?
pool.explain: Practise, then sleep. Staying up cuts sleep, and sleep alone stores nothing new.

pool.prompt: When should you stop playing tablet games before lights out?
choices: You do not need to stop
pool.hint: Games keep your brain busy. How long does it need to wind down?
pool.explain: About an hour before lights out, so you fall asleep more easily.

pool.prompt: You sleep {n} hours every night for {k} nights. How many hours of sleep is that?
pool.hint: {n} hours each night, for {k} nights. Multiply.
pool.explain: {n} times {k} is {=n*k} hours. Every one of those nights helps store what you practised.

choices: A quick check in the morning of what you practised
Doing the same page again at midnight
pool.hint: Which one does not cut your sleep?
pool.explain: A quick morning check shows what you kept. The other two cut your sleep.

pool.prompt: A tablet game lasts {n} minutes and must end 60 minutes before lights out. How many minutes before lights out must it start?
pool.hint: Add the {n} minutes of the game to the 60 screen-free minutes.
pool.explain: {n} + 60 = {=n+60} minutes before lights out. The screen-free hour helps you fall asleep.
